9.

The onus to prove this issue was upon the petitioner and to prove that she suffered grievous injuries in this accident on account of rashness and negligence on the part of respondent no. 1, she examined herself as PW1 and tendered her evidence by way of affidavit Ex.PW1/A. Petitioner as PW1 deposed that on 05.11.2023 she was travelling in e-rickshaw, which she took from Samaypur Badli Metro Station and going to Jain Colony.

She was the single passenger in above said e-rickshaw, when the said e-rickshaw reached near Shiv Chowk, Shahbad dairy, the driver of said e- rickshaw parked his e-rickshaw near left hand side to the road side and went to buy some goods and just came back with in few minutes and after returning back the driver started his e-rickshaw and when going suddenly a vehicle hit their e-rickshaw from the back and due to such impact she was crashed into the front seat of said e-rickshaw and sustained injuries.
She was removed to Dr. BSA Hospital for treatment wherein she was treated vide MLC no. 14667/23.

Though, PW1 / petitioner has been cross examined by the respondents but nothing material has come on record to disbelieve the testimony of PW1/petitioner, as being injured she is natural eye-witness of accident.

Apart from deposition of PW1, the fact that petitioner suffered injuries in the accident is also supported by her MLC filed along with DAR collectively Ex. PW1/1, Respondent no. 1 has not placed on record any document to disprove the factum of rash and negligent driving by him and even as stated above settled connected case.

2025.07.10 MACT No. 85/24 Page 6 +0530 16:37:49 "The general purport of the words res ipsa loquitur is that the accident "speaks for itself" or tell's its own story.
There are cases in which the accident speaks for itself so that it is sufficient for the plaintiff to prove the accident and nothing more.
It will then be for the defendant to establish that the accident happened due to some other cause than his own negligence.

Salmond on the Law of Torts (15th Ed.) at p. 306 states:
"The maxim res ipsa loquitur applies whenever it is so improbable that such an accident would have happened without the negligence of the defendant that a reasonable jury could find without further evidence that it was so caused."

In Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd Ed., Vol. 28, at p. 77, the position is stated thus: "An exception to the general rule that the burden of proof of the alleged negligence is in the first instance on the plaintiff occurs wherever the facts already established are such that .the proper and natural inference arising from them is ,that the injury complained of was caused by the defendant's negligence, or where the event charged Paridhi vs Kapil Sharma on 10 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/60078527/
5 as negligence "tells its own story' of negligence on the part of the defendant, the story so told being clear and unambiguous."

Further, relying upon the judgment of Mahila Dhanvanti and Ors Vs. Phulwant Mahendra Singh,
Miscellaneous Appeal no.239/1992 decided by Hon'ble Madhya Pradesh High Court on 29.07.1993 in which it is held as under:-
"The plaintiff can prove the accident but cannot prove how it happened to establish negligence.

sentences.text: This hardship is to be avoided by applying the principle of res ipsa loquitur.
The general purport of the words res ipsa loquitur is that the accident speaks for itself or tells its own story".
Thus, Claims Tribunal while dealing with the law of torts in motor accident cases applies the principle of "res ipsa loquitur".

Considering all this, it stands proved that accident in question occurred due to rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle by the respondent no. 1 and petitioner suffered grievous injuries in the said accident.
Accordingly, issue no. 1 is decided in favour of petitioner and against the respondents.

sentences.text: Whether the petitioner is entitled to compensation if so, what amount and from whom of respondents?

OPP. 
10.

As far as the issue with respect to right to claim compensation is concerned, being injured,
petitioner is the natural eye-witness of accident and is well within her rights to claim compensation from the respondents.
Accordingly, the question of right of the injured for claiming of compensation is decided in favour of the petitioner.

Now, the second part of the issue in hand with respect to the quantum of compensation is to be adjudicated and below are the finding: -
11.
Petitioner as PW1 deposed that after the accident she was taken to Dr. BSA Hospital wherein she was treated vide MLC no. 14667/23.
It is further deposed by PW1 that she was working as primary teacher and was getting Rs. 20,000/- per month as salary.

She further deposed that she incurred about Rs. 50,000/- on her treatment and medicines, Rs. 20,000/- towards transport charges, Rs.
50,000/- on special liquid diets and claimed a compensation of Rs. 5 lakhs.
Though, petitioner has claimed that she has spent Rs. 50,000/- on her medical treatment but no medical bills have been placed and proved on record.
Admittedly, petitioner got her treatment from government hospital.
Accordingly, no amount is awarded to the petitioner on this head.

Further, there is no evidence to verify that petitioner has spent any amount on special diet, conveyance, attendant etc., however,
keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the petitioner, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner must have undergone surgeries and procedures and thus he must have incurred Paridhi vs Kapil Sharma on 10 July, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/60078527/
6 expenses on special diet required for her speedy recovery as well as on travel to hospitals etc.
Accordingly, Rs.15,000/- each towards special diet and conveyance is awarded to the petitioner/injured.

Digitally signed by SUNIL SUNIL KUMAR KUMAR Date:
2025.07.10 Paridhi Vs. Kapil Sharma & Ors. 16:37:58 +0530 MACT No. 85/24 Page 8 12.
Considering the testimony of PW1 and long treatment record of petitioner, it is presumed that petitioner could not continue her work during her treatment i.e. about 3 months.
Except deposition of petitioner, there is no document which proves that petitioner was earning Rs. 20,000/- per month.
During the arguments, it was the contention of Ld. Counsel for respondents that petitioner was not doing anything for gain and even as per her own statement given to the police she is housewife.

No doubt, petitioner could not prove on record that she was working as teacher or earning Rs.20,000/- per month but services of house wife towards handling household work and taking care of family in all respect cannot be negated as skilled labour.

In such scenario,
compensation amount towards monthly loss of dependency is to be computed on the basis of minimum wages of skilled labour, which were Rs. 21,215/-.

Accordingly, a sum of Rs.63,645/-
(21,215x3) for loss of income during the period of her treatment for 3 months and during this period she must have taken the services of an attendant and hence a sum of Rs.15,000/- (5000x3) for 3 months, towards attendant charges are awarded to the petitioner.
13. Further, apart from the above mentioned amounts, petitioner is entitled for compensation regarding mental pain and suffering, disfiguration etc.

Accordingly, after giving due weight-age to the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, a sum of Rs.50,000/- for mental pain and physical shock as well as for pain and suffering due to this accident, Rs. 50,000/- towards loss of amenities of life and Rs.50,000/- for loss of inconvenience, hardship disappointment, frustration,
mention stress dejectment and unhappiness in future life etc. are also awarded to the petitioner,
making a total sum of Rs. 2,58,645/-, details of which is mentioned in the attached proforma.

Co. is liable to indemnify the insured and to pay the compensation to the petitioner against which Ins. Co. is given right to recover the compensation amount from the respondent no. 1 / driver and respondent no. 2 / registered owner jointly and severally but after paying compensation to the petitioner.

Relying upon judgment in Pushpabai Purshottam Udeshi & Ors vs Ranjit Ginning & Pressing Co. (P) Ltd. & Anr. 1977 (2) SCC 745 Civil Appeal No. 2071 of 1968, decided on March 25, 1977 by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India wherein it was held as under: - Digitally signed by SUNIL SUNIL KUMAR Paridhi Vs. Kapil Sharma & Ors.
There are cases in which the accident speaks for itself so that it is sufficient for the plaintiff to prove the accident and nothing more.
It will then be for the defendant to establish that the accident happened due to some other cause than his own negligence.
This hardship is to be avoided by applying the principle of res ipsa loquitur.
The general purport of the words res ipsa loquitur is that the accident speaks for itself or tells its own story".
Thus, Claims Tribunal while dealing with the law of torts in motor accident cases applies the principle of "res ipsa loquitur".
As far as the issue with respect to right to claim compensation is concerned, being injured,
petitioner is the natural eye-witness of accident and is well within her rights to claim compensation from the respondents.
Considering the testimony of PW1 and long treatment record of petitioner, it is presumed that petitioner could not continue her work during her treatment i.e. about 3 months.
